payload.body: Asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the ratio of the rising phase duration to the falling phase duration of the first derivative of the glottal flow waveform. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal cycle is partitioned into the rising phase (where g'(n) is positive, from minimum to maximum) and the falling phase (where g'(n) is negative, from maximum to minimum); the asymmetry coefficient is rising-phase duration / falling-phase duration. A coefficient near 1 indicates a symmetric pulse (typical modal phonation), while deviation from 1 indicates asymmetric closure — a longer falling phase (coefficient < 1) marks abrupt closure in pressed phonation, and a longer rising phase (coefficient > 1) indicates gradual closure in breathy phonation. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking which frames the cycle, (3) the first derivative of g(n) to locate phase boundaries. It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; maintained reference ranges separate typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed from the glottogram by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and maintained alongside the maximum-flow-derivative, the glottal-flow-declination-rate, the phase quotients, and the other glottal source parameters as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: the asymmetry coefficient reported in a laryngology study comparing pressed and breathy phonation types; the asymmetry coefficient computed from a glottal-flow waveform in a laryngeal dysphonia case; the asymmetry coefficient value of 0.85 measured in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (the steepest negative slope, not a ratio); maximum-flow-derivative (the peak positive slope, not a ratio) [formal: coeficiens inaequalitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: modal-phonation
payload.scope: A human-made classification category made by laryngology and speech science to name the normal periodic mode of phonation so that breathy and creaky voice can be classified as deviations from it in clinical assessment and voice training.

definition.body: Modal phonation is the normal periodic mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: the mode in which the vocal folds vibrate with complete glottal closure each cycle, at a stable fundamental frequency within the speaker's modal range, producing periodic excitation of the vocal tract. It is the reference mode of the taxonomy: breathy and creaky phonation are defined against it, as deviations in closure and cycle character. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - medial adduction with complete closure each cycle (a high closure quotient) and firm contact, (2) the cycle signature - a stable f0 in the modal range with periodic, non-implosive cycles and no flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature - a clean periodic tone with a strong harmonic series and minimal aperiodic noise. It persists as the reference mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: named in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice assessment (a breathy or creaky quality is classified as a deviation from modal) and in voice training (restoring or maintaining the modal mode), and maintained alongside the other modes in Sundberg's phonation inventory. e.g.: the modal-phonation mode in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the 'modal voice' category on a voice therapy plan for a patient with habitual breathy voice; the 'modal voice' label in a phonetic description of a speaker's neutral sustained /a/ | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with turbulent noise leak); creaky voice (low-f0 aperiodic implosive cycles); whisper (unvoiced glottal airflow) [formal: vox modalis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

It requires the glottal-cycle as its operational window: the per-cycle T0 frames the pitch-synchronous analysis, and the derivative is computed only within the boundaries of each cycle (from onset to the return to baseline). Remove the glottal-cycle construct: the MFD measure loses its per-cycle framing and cannot operate. NHR quantifies the share of noise energy relative to harmonic energy in a voiced speech signal. payload.name: diplophonic-voice
payload.scope: A human-made classification category made by laryngology and speech science to name the bimodal-f0 phonation mode so it can be told apart from modal phonation in clinical assessment and voice training.

definition.body: Diplophonic voice (diplophonia) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a bimodal fundamental frequency: the two vocal folds vibrate simultaneously at two different frequencies because they are asymmetric in mass, stiffness, or length, so each fold oscillates at its own f0 and the voice carries two coexisting pitch tracks separated by a beat frequency. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - asymmetric vibration of the two folds (unequal mass, stiffness, or adduction), (2) the cycle signature - two fundamental frequencies f0a and f0b, bimodal pitch with a beat at the absolute difference of the two f0s, (3) the acoustic signature - a rough, dual-pitched, double-voice timbre with two resolvable pitch tracks. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (diplophonia as a marker of asymmetric fold pathology such as unilateral paresis or a fold mass) and in voice training, and maintained alongside the other voice modes in Sundberg's phonation inventory. e.g.: diplophonia labeled as a bimodal-f0 voice in a voice-disorder assessment of a patient with a vocal fold mass; the two-fundamental-frequency voice in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the diplophonic quality in a laryngology report for a patient with unilateral vocal fold paresis | not: modal phonation (a single stable f0 with symmetric folds); breathy voice (turbulent noise leak, not a second pitch track); creaky voice (low-f0 aperiodic implosive cycles) [formal: vox duplex | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: intensity
payload.scope: A standardized acoustic power measure built to quantify loudness level and vocal effort in clinical voice assessment and signal-processing practice.

definition.body: Intensity is the acoustic power per unit area carried by a sound wave, quantified as the time-averaged product of acoustic pressure and particle velocity at a point in the medium. In speech and voice analysis it is computed from the microphone-recorded signal as the mean-square pressure over a short analysis window, expressed in decibels relative to the reference pressure of 20 micropascals (the standard threshold of human hearing). Parameters: (1) the acoustic pressure signal p(t) — the waveform captured by a calibrated microphone, (2) the analysis window length (typically 20–50 ms for voiced speech segments), (3) the reference pressure p0 = 20 µPa for dB conversion. Persistence mechanism: the standardized acoustic parameter measured from recorded voice signals, implemented in voice-analysis software and reported in clinical laryngology measurement standards. e.g.: intensity of a sustained vowel in a voice-disorder baseline assessment; intensity contour across syllables in an LMTD protocol; intensity reported in dB SPL alongside jitter and shimmer in MDVP reports | not: sound-pressure level; loudness [formal: intensitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Parameters: (1) the acoustic pressure signal p(t) — the waveform captured by a calibrated microphone, (2) the analysis window length (typically 20–50 ms for voiced speech segments), (3) the reference pressure p0 = 20 µPa for dB conversion. Persistence mechanism: the standardized acoustic parameter measured from recorded voice signals, implemented in voice-analysis software and reported in clinical laryngology measurement standards. e.g.: intensity of a sustained vowel in a voice-disorder baseline assessment; intensity contour across syllables in an LMTD protocol; intensity reported in dB SPL alongside jitter and shimmer in MDVP reports | not: sound-pressure level; loudness [formal: intensitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: acoustic-voice-quality-index
payload.scope: A standardized composite clinical measure built to quantify overall voice quality by combining multiple acoustic parameters into a single scalar index for objective voice-disorder screening.

definition.body: Acoustic voice quality index (AVQ) is a composite clinical measure that combines several voice-quality acoustic parameters into a single scalar index quantifying the overall deviation from typical voice. Computed as a weighted linear combination of the logarithm of shimmer (normalized amplitude quotient), the logarithm of jitter (period perturbation), and the noise-to-harmonics ratio: AVQ = α·ln(NQI) + β·ln(jitter) + γ·ln(NHR), where α, β, γ are empirically derived regression weights. Parameters: (1) the component parameters — NQI, jitter, and NHR, each measured from the same voiced speech segment, (2) the regression weights — derived from discriminant analysis of a reference population of typical versus disordered voices. Persistence mechanism: the standardized composite index documented in clinical voice literature, implemented in the GRBAS-based voice analysis protocol and in laryngology assessment software, maintained alongside the GRBAS scale and the CAPE-V. e.g.: AVQ score used to differentiate typical from dysphonic voices in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; AVQ computed from sustained /a/ and running speech in the GRBAS assessment protocol; AVQ reported as a screening threshold in the CAPES-V voice-disorder study | not: GRBAS; CAPE-V [formal: index vocis sonans qualitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-flow-derivative
payload.scope: A standardized signal-processing construct representing the first time derivative of the glottal flow waveform, built to provide the fundamental rate-of-change measure underlying glottal-closure dynamics parameters.

definition.body: Glottal flow derivative is the first time derivative of the glottal flow waveform g(t), quantifying the instantaneous rate of change of glottal airflow. Computed numerically from the sampled glottal-flow estimate g(n) as the first difference g(n+1) - g(n), optionally normalized by the sampling interval to yield units of volume per second. The positive branch (derivative > 0) corresponds to the opening phase of the glottal cycle; the negative branch (derivative < 0) corresponds to the closing phase. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the sampling interval Δt from the signal's sampling rate, (3) the numerical differentiation method (forward, backward, or central difference). Persistence mechanism: the standardized signal-processing construct implemented in voice-analysis software, documented in the Klatt and Klatt glottal-source parameter set, and maintained as the foundational derivative measure from which glottal-flow-declination-rate and maximum-flow-derivative are derived. e.g.: glottal-flow derivative used as the input to glottal-flow-declination-rate computation in the Dewaele parameter set; glottal-flow derivative waveform displayed in a Praat glottogram analysis panel; glottal-flow derivative computed from an EGG-based glottogram in a voice-disorder assessment of vocal fold paralysis | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (a derived scalar, not the full derivative function); maximum-flow-derivative (a derived scalar, not the full derivative function) [formal: derivata fluminis glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: hammarberg-index
payload.scope: A standardized clinical index built to quantify glottal efficiency during phonation by relating subglottal pressure to phonatory flow, built to persist as a measure of vocal effort and voice-disorder severity.

definition.body: Hammarberg index is a voice-quality measure quantifying the ratio of mean subglottal pressure to mean flow during phonation, used as an estimate of glottal adduction efficiency. Computed as the ratio of mean subglottal pressure (measured via occlusion pressure or esophageal balloon) to mean peak-to-peak glottal flow (measured via pneumotachograph or inverse filtering of the acoustic signal). The formula is HI = Psub / Fflow, where Psub is mean subglottal pressure in cmH2O and Fflow is mean airflow in L/s during sustained vowel phonation. Parameters: (1) the subglottal pressure measurement method — occlusion pressure (valsalva maneuver) or esophageal balloon, (2) the airflow measurement method — pneumotachograph or inverse-filtering estimate, (3) the phonation task — typically sustained /a/ at comfortable pitch and loudness. A higher HI indicates greater subglottal pressure for a given flow, suggesting incomplete glottal closure (breathy phonation) or compensatory effort; a lower HI indicates efficient glottal closure. Persistence mechanism: the standardized index documented in laryngology literature, implemented in voice-laboratory measurement protocols, and maintained alongside other glottal efficiency measures. e.g.: Hammarberg index measured from a sustained /a/ in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; Hammarberg index reported in a laryngology case series on vocal fold paralysis; Hammarberg index used as a treatment-outcome measure in a voice-therapy protocol | not: phonation-threshold-pressure (the minimum pressure needed to initiate phonation, not a ratio during phonation); glottal-efficiency-index (a related but distinct composite measure) [formal: index Hammarberg | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vf3
payload.scope: A standardized acoustic parameter representing the third formant frequency, built to persist as a diagnostic measure of vocal-tract shape and resonance characteristics in voice-disorder assessment.

definition.body: VF3 (formant F3) is the third formant frequency of the vocal-tract transfer function, quantified as the third spectral peak in the voice signal's frequency spectrum after removing the glottal source. Computed from the linear-prediction coefficients of the voiced speech signal or directly from the power spectrum of the pre-emphasized signal. Parameters: (1) the analysis method — linear predictive coding (LPC) order typically 12–16 for adult speakers, or spectral peak-picking on the power spectrum, (2) the voicing segment — typically a sustained vowel with stable vocal-tract configuration, (3) the speaker's sex and age group — which determine expected F3 range (typically 2500–3500 Hz for adult males, 3000–4500 Hz for adult females). VF3 is diagnostically relevant for distinguishing normal from disordered resonance, particularly in hypernasality and hyponasality assessment. Persistence mechanism: the standardized parameter implemented in voice-analysis software (Praat, MDVP), documented in laryngology measurement protocols, and maintained as a member of the formant analysis parameter set. e.g.: VF3 measured from a sustained /i/ vowel in a cleft-palate hypernasality assessment; VF3 reported alongside F1 and F2 in a voice-disorder classification study; VF3 used to characterize resonance changes in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia treatment protocol | not: formant-dispersion (the spread between formants, not a single formant frequency); F0 (fundamental frequency, not a vocal-tract resonance) [formal: F3 | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

replacementSpec.body: The spectral centroid is a human-made measure used in signal and audio processing that quantifies the center of mass of a spectrum's magnitude distribution — the point at which the energy of the spectrum would balance if it were a physical object. It is computed as the weighted mean of the frequency components, where the weights are the magnitudes at each frequency, and is typically expressed in Hertz. The spectral centroid serves as a proxy for the perceptual attribute of brightness in sound, since higher centroids correspond to more high-frequency energy. payload.name: diplophonic-voice
payload.scope: A human-made classification category made by laryngology and speech science to name the two-pitched double-voice mode of phonation so it can be told apart from the other phonation modes in clinical assessment and voice training.

definition.body: Diplophonic voice is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds vibrate asymmetrically — one fold more adducted, stiffer, or shorter — so that two distinct fundamental frequencies coexist in the sound (a bimodal fundamental, often octave- or subharmonic-related) and the folds vibrate out of phase, producing the audible two-pitched, rough double-voice quality. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — asymmetric adduction, stiffness, or mass between the two folds, (2) the cycle signature — two coexisting fundamental frequencies with out-of-phase fold vibration, (3) the acoustic signature — a two-pitched, rough double-voice timbre with a bimodal fundamental-frequency contour. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics (the fifth mode of Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory), used in voice-disorder assessment (diplophonia as a clinical marker of unilateral vocal-fold paresis or an asymmetric mass) and in voice training (the two-pitched sound at the chest-to-head voice transition), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: a two-pitched double voice in a patient with left vocal-fold paresis, labeled diplophonic in a laryngology report; the diplophonic mode in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the rough two-pitched sound a singer passes through at the chest-to-head voice transition, labeled diplophonia | not: creaky voice (a single low fundamental with implosive cycles, one oscillator); modal phonation (a single periodic fundamental); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, no fundamental) [formal: vox duplex | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics (the fifth mode of Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory), used in voice-disorder assessment (diplophonia as a clinical marker of unilateral vocal-fold paresis or an asymmetric mass) and in voice training (the two-pitched sound at the chest-to-head voice transition), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: a two-pitched double voice in a patient with left vocal-fold paresis, labeled diplophonic in a laryngology report; the diplophonic mode in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the rough two-pitched sound a singer passes through at the chest-to-head voice transition, labeled diplophonia | not: creaky voice (a single low fundamental with implosive cycles, one oscillator); modal phonation (a single periodic fundamental); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, no fundamental) [formal: vox duplex | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: stroboscopy
payload.scope: Clinicians made stroboscopy to visualize vocal fold mucosal wave and vibratory symmetry — information invisible at real-time observation — so they can detect subtle mucosal pathology that affects voice quality.

definition.body: Stroboscopy is a clinical visualization technique that uses synchronized flashing light to create a slow-motion effect for observing vocal fold vibration during phonation. A strobe light flashes at a frequency matched to the patient's fundamental frequency (f0) from pitch tracking, so that each flash illuminates the vocal folds at the same phase of their vibratory cycle. The accumulated visual perception is a slowed or stationary view of the periodic motion, enabling clinicians to assess mucosal wave propagation, vibratory amplitude, symmetry, and phase closure. Parameters: (1) the excitation source — a flexible laryngeal stroboscope or flexible laryngoscope with integrated strobe LED, (2) the fundamental frequency measurement from the patient's voice, (3) the strobe synchronization — phase-locked flashing to f0, (4) the visual observation — mucosal wave, symmetry, and phase closure assessed during sustained vowel production. It persists as a standardized clinical procedure in laryngology practice and voice-disorder assessment, documented in laryngology textbooks and clinical protocols. e.g.: the flexible stroboscopy examination in a laryngology clinic for a patient with vocal nodules; the macrostroboscopic view of mucosal wave propagation in a laryngology textbook figure; the semi-automated strobogram analysis of vocal fold vibration symmetry reported in a voice-surgery outcome study | not: direct laryngoscopy (a static anatomical view without synchronized illumination); videolaryngoscopy (high-speed camera recording of true-time vibration, not stroboscopic slow-motion) [formal: stroboscopya | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: high-speed-videolaryngoscopy
payload.scope: Researchers made high-speed videolaryngoscopy to record vocal fold vibration at true temporal resolution — capturing rapid subglottal events, collision dynamics, and asymmetries that stroboscopy aliases or blurs — so they can study vibratory mechanics that require real-time recording.

definition.body: High-speed videolaryngoscopy (HSV) is a clinical imaging technique that records vocal fold vibration at high frame rates (typically 2000-4000 frames per second) using a high-speed camera coupled to a rigid or flexible laryngoscope. Unlike stroboscopy, which relies on the strobe aliasing effect, HSV captures each frame of the glottal cycle at true time resolution, enabling direct visualization of mucosal wave propagation, collision dynamics, asymmetry, and phase closure without the aliasing artifacts of stroboscopy. Parameters: (1) the high-speed camera — capable of ≥2000 fps at sufficient spatial resolution, (2) the laryngoscope — rigid 70-degree or flexible fiberoptic endoscope with integrated illumination, (3) the illumination — coherent LED or xenon light for adequate signal-to-noise at high speed, (4) the recording — digital storage of continuous high-frame-rate video during sustained phonation. It persists as a research and clinical tool in advanced voice laboratories, documented in laryngology research protocols and biomechanics literature. e.g.: the 4000 fps high-speed video recording of vocal fold collision dynamics in a laryngeal biomechanics paper; the HSV examination of unilateral vocal fold paralysis in a laryngology research study; the high-speed cinematic analysis of mucosal wave propagation reported in a voice-surgery outcome paper | not: stroboscopy (synchronized strobe slow-motion, not true-time recording); standard videolaryngoscopy (real-time video at 30-60 fps, too slow for individual cycle resolution) [formal: video-laryngoscopya velocissimus | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cape-v
payload.scope: Speech-language pathologists made CAPE-V to standardize how trained raters assess voice disorder severity using a 6-dimension perceptual scale — replacing subjective global ratings with a structured, reproducible protocol that anchors each severity level to specific exemplar recordings.

definition.body: CAPE-V (Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice) is a standardized perceptual voice-assessment protocol in which a trained rater listens to voice samples and rates the presence and severity of six voice attributes on a 0-100 visual analog scale. The six dimensions are: (1) roughness, (2) breathiness, (3) strain, (4) pitch loudness, (5) pitch, and (6) loudness. Each dimension is rated independently, and the total severity score is the mean across the six dimensions. The rater listens to sustained vowels and connected speech passages. Parameters: (1) the voice samples — sustained /a/ and connected speech, (2) the six rated dimensions with their anchor definitions, (3) the 0-100 visual analog scale per dimension, (4) the severity scoring protocol (mean across six dimensions). It persists as a standardized clinical protocol maintained by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, taught in graduate voice assessment curricula, and used in clinical research protocols. e.g.: the CAPE-V protocol applied by a SLP to rate severity of dysphonia in a head and neck cancer outcome study; the CAPE-V roughness subscale rating of a post-thyroidectomy voice; the CAPE-V severity profile (all six dimensions) reported in a voice-surgery pre/post comparison | not: GRBAS (a 5-dimension ordinal scale with fixed anchors 0-3, not a VAS protocol); the VHI-10 (a patient self-report questionnaire, not a trained-rater perceptual protocol) [formal: vocis perceptualis aestimatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]
